soundness_argument:
The change is in TypeStore.unifiable(_:_:extending:handlingCoercionsWith:), TypeStore.swift:1006-1009 and 1061-1099. It runs only after the shared prefix: substitution walk, a == b, the variable cases and the TypeAlias cases on either side. Those paths are untouched, so a variable against anything and an alias against its aliasee still take the original route. When `unify` is on, the 20-case `switch (self[a], self[b])` is replaced by unifiableSameShape, followed by the same `result || areCoercible(a, b)`.

Why it is exactly equivalent (release build):
(1) The set of TypeTree conformers is closed. All of them are value types in Sources/FrontEnd/Types: Arrow, AssociatedType, Bundle, Enum, EqualityWitness, ErrorType, FunctionPointer, GenericParameter, Implication, LiteralType, MachineType, Metakind, Metatype, Namespace, OpaqueType, RemoteType, Struct, Trait, Tuple, TypeAlias, TypeApplication, TypeVariable, TypeWitness and UniversalType. A grep finds no conformer outside that directory and no class.
(2) self[n] returns the payload of an `any TypeTree` (TypeStore.swift:733-746). Its dynamic type is always one of these concrete value types, never a nested box, Optional or subclass. So `v as X` succeeds iff ObjectIdentifier(type(of: v)) == ObjectIdentifier(X.self), and the `as!` on y can never trap.
(3) So the original tuple switch reaches a per-kind unifiable(t,u) iff both operands have the same dynamic type and that kind is one of the 11 structural kinds: Arrow, AssociatedType, Bundle, EqualityWitness, FunctionPointer, Implication, Metatype, RemoteType, Tuple, TypeApplication, UniversalType. In every other case it yields false: same-kind nominal or atomic types via explicit `false` cases, different kinds via `default`. The new code yields exactly this. On a tag mismatch it returns false before any cast, and the original default branch does no SubstitutionTable mutation either. On a match it calls the same per-kind function with the same arguments in the same order. Case order is irrelevant because the patterns are disjoint.
(4) The per-kind functions, the coercion handler call and its short-circuit position are unchanged. The order of substitution side effects is therefore identical, and the recursive calls re-enter the same function and re-read the same flag.
(5) Unreachable kinds behave the same. TypeVariable cannot reach the dispatch: it is only materialised when n.isVariable, which is handled earlier. Two different TypeAlias values cannot reach it either, because the alias case recurses first.

Precondition and caveat: the equivalence holds when assertions are disabled, as in the release-built frozen oracle. In a debug build (-Onone, assertions on) the baseline's `default: assert(tag(of: a) != tag(of: b))` fires when two distinct LiteralType values are unified, since LiteralType has no case in the original switch. That input is reachable from user code: takeInt(b) with b: Builtin.FloatingPointLiteral, in u01-literal-types.hylo. The flagged path returns false there instead of trapping. This is a debug-only divergence where the baseline is the broken side (an assertion crash). I derived it from the code only, because building a debug compiler is not allowed here.

verified.evidence: TypeStore.swift:1050-1052, baseline `default: assert(tag(of: a) != tag(of: b)); result = false`. LiteralType (cases integer and float) is the only TypeTree kind that can reach the dispatch with equal tags but has no case of its own. TypeVariable and TypeAlias are handled before the switch. The input is reachable: /home/user/hylo-new/research/review/unify/u01-literal-types.hylo (takeInt(b) with b: Builtin.FloatingPointLiteral) produces 'cannot pass value of type FloatingPointLiteral to parameter IntegerLiteral' in the release oracle, so unification of IntegerLiteral against FloatingPointLiteral is attempted. Under assertions (swift build/test default debug) the baseline would trap there, and unifiableSameShape returns false (default branch, TypeStore.swift:1094-1097). In the release oracle both are identical (oracle-run2.txt). This is derived from the code; I did not run a debug build.
verified.suggested_fix: Fix the baseline: add `case (_ as LiteralType, _ as LiteralType): result = false` to the original switch, or drop the assert. Mention this in REPORT.md so that the soundness claim states it is checked in release mode only.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute the finding. It is confirmed from the code and from the release oracle, but I did not reproduce the trap: no debug binary exists (.build has only release builds, and building is forbidden).

1) The baseline is missing a case. I listed every `TypeTree` conformer in Sources/FrontEnd: GenericParameter, LiteralType, MachineType, OpaqueType, Tuple, Arrow, AssociatedType, Bundle, Enum, EqualityWitness, ErrorType, FunctionPointer, Implication, Metakind, Metatype, Namespace, RemoteType, Struct, Trait, TypeAlias, TypeApplication, TypeVariable, TypeWitness, UniversalType. TypeVariable is handled by the `isVariable` checks and TypeAlias by the alias checks before the switch (TypeStore.swift:988-1001). Every other kind has a same-kind case in the baseline switch (TypeStore.swift:1010-1052) except LiteralType. Two distinct LiteralType values (`.integer` and `.float`) have the same tag, so they fall into `default: assert(tag(of: a) != tag(of: b))`, and that assert fails.

2) The input is reachable. `resolve(builtin:)` gives `Builtin.IntegerLiteral` and `Builtin.FloatingPointLiteral` their LiteralType metatypes (Typer.swift:4564). For an argument, the solver's `solve(coercion:)` calls `typer.coerced`, whose fast path calls `program.types.unifiable(head, goal)` with dealiased operands (Typer.swift:4213). The operands here are distinct, closed LiteralType identities, so the call goes past the equality, variable and alias checks into the shape dispatch. I re-ran the oracle on /home/user/hylo-new/research/review/unify/u01-literal-types.hylo: config `unify` prints "1/1 identical". The baseline dump (/home/user/hylo-new/research/review/unify/verify-unify-1/base.txt) shows "cannot pass value of type 'FloatingPointLiteral' to parameter 'IntegerLiteral'" at lines 15 and 17, and the reverse message at line 16. That fits a failed fast-path unify followed by a failed slow path.

3) The divergence exists only with assertions on. In release, `assert` is compiled out, so the baseline returns `false || areCoercible(a, b)`. The unify path's `unifiableSameShape` sees equal tags, matches no case, takes its `default` (returns false), and then also returns `result || areCoercible(a, b)`. In release the two paths are identical. In a debug build (`swift build` / `swift test`) the baseline would trap and the unify path would not.

So "kind: baseline-bug, severity minor" is accurate. The bug is in the baseline. It does not count against the unify flag's soundness, but the soundness claim should say it was checked on release builds only.
verdict.fix: Fix the baseline rather than the experiment. In TypeStore.swift's `unifiable(_:_:extending:handlingCoercionsWith:)` switch, add `case (_ as LiteralType, _ as LiteralType): result = false` next to the other atomic kinds (MachineType, Metakind, ...). Distinct literal types are never syntactically unifiable, and identical ones were already caught by `a == b`. Keep the `default: assert(tag(of: a) != tag(of: b))` so that a kind added later without a case still trips in debug builds. The `unifiableSameShape` default needs no change; at most add a comment that LiteralType is one of the atomic kinds it covers. Optionally add a negative test that passes a `Builtin.FloatingPointLiteral` to a `Builtin.IntegerLiteral` parameter, which exercises the case under `swift test`. In REPORT.md, note that the oracle checks are release-mode only, and that this was the one debug-only divergence found.

verdict.reasoning:
The mechanism is real. The profile evidence for its size is not.

Source: in TypeStore.swift:1063-1097, `unifiableSameShape` compares `ObjectIdentifier(type(of:))` of the two operands and then does `switch x` with 11 `case let t as K` patterns, in this order: TypeApplication, Arrow, Tuple, EqualityWitness, AssociatedType, Bundle, FunctionPointer, Implication, Metatype, RemoteType, UniversalType. The other kinds fall to `default: return false`. Those are Struct, Trait, Enum, GenericParameter, MachineType, Namespace, OpaqueType, ErrorType, Metakind, TypeWitness and LiteralType. Two operands of such a kind that are equal-tag but not identical (for example Int vs Bool, or two different traits or generic parameters) therefore go through all 11 failed patterns before `default`.

Machine code: I disassembled the frozen oracle binary (research/exp/bin/4587ce9e1a23/tc-bench.real, symbol at 0x38dc70). The listing is saved at /home/user/hylo-new/research/review/unify/verify-unify-2/unifiableSameShape.asm. The body contains 21 `call swift_dynamicCast` and 12 calls to the outlined existential copy `$s8FrontEnd8TypeTree_pWOc`. Each case first copies the `any TypeTree` existential, then calls swift_dynamicCast on it. A success makes a second cast for the forced `y as! K`. So the default path really does pay about 11 existential copies plus 11 failed runtime casts, after 2 `getDynamicType` calls. On top of that, the caller makes two `as? TypeAlias` casts at lines 997-1001 before this function runs.

Not a regression: the baseline tuple switch (lines 1010-1056) is worse on the same inputs. It builds a tuple of two existentials and tries up to about 20 pair patterns. So this is leftover cost the optimization does not remove, and soundness is not affected.

Overstated evidence: the 4.35% self time for tryCast and the 18% inclusive time for swift_dynamicCast in research/profile/allon.txt cannot be attributed to `unifiable`. The profile has no caller edges, and neither `unifiable` nor `unifiableSameShape` appears anywhere in its inclusive list, which stops at about 8.9%. The casts most visible there come with SyntaxFilter.callAsFunction, Program.annotation and Program.symbol(annotating:) at about 13% each, which are syntax-side casts. REPORT §5.2 shows a ceiling: `unify` alone cut the stdlib run from 461 to 426 ms (about 8%), and that covered all of the shape-dispatch overhead. What remains on the nominal-mismatch path is some unknown fraction of that, likely a few percent at most.

So the finding is confirmed as a real missed constant-factor improvement, but at minor/low priority. I took no timings, as the rules require.
verdict.fix:
The fix decides the kind from `tx`, which is already computed, before any cast. It also replaces the checked cast for the second operand with an unchecked one once the tags are known equal.

1. Right after `if tx != ObjectIdentifier(type(of: y)) { return false }`, add an early exit for the atomic kinds. One option is a chain of pointer comparisons such as `if tx == ObjectIdentifier(Struct.self) || tx == ObjectIdentifier(Trait.self) || tx == ObjectIdentifier(GenericParameter.self) || ... { return false }`. Another is a precomputed `static let structural: Set<ObjectIdentifier>` of the 11 structural kinds, with `guard structural.contains(tx) else { return false }`. The pointer chain avoids hashing.

2. For the structural kinds, branch on `tx == ObjectIdentifier(K.self)` in order of observed frequency (TypeApplication, Arrow, Tuple first). Then do the one cast, `x as! K`, plus `unsafeDowncast`-style access for y, or a `withExistential`/`_openExistential` helper, so the tag is not re-checked.

3. Longer term (REPORT §5.2 'next step'): store a dense `UInt8` kind array parallel to `types` in TypeStore. Both `tag(of:)` and this dispatch would then need no existential projection, and the `as? TypeAlias` checks at TypeStore.swift:997-1001 could become cheap kind tests too.

Before landing: semtest must stay dump-identical, since the change only reorders pure dispatch. Check with `tc-bench --count` and a sampling profile that has caller edges, so the gain is attributed to `unifiable` and not to the syntax-side casts (SyntaxFilter/Program.annotation) that dominate swift_dynamicCast in allon.txt.

soundness_argument:
Claim: with flag `index`, summon(_:in:where:then:penalties:) (indexedSummon) and canDeriveCoercions give the same results, in the same order and with the same penalties, as the unindexed algorithm. No counterexample was found. Preconditions:
(P1) The index is used only when declarationsOnStack is empty, so notOnStack filters nothing. The visible set then equals the full givens(visibleFrom:), which is stable: givens(lexicallyIn:) is memoised, imports/moduleToGivens are memoised, there is no cache invalidation anywhere, and empty groups are dropped in both the index and the baseline. So scopeToGivenIndex can be cached safely, and redirecting a scope with no lexical givens to its parent gives identical groups.
(P2) No coercion source is visible from scopeOfUse, i.e. no given whose head is a bare context parameter or an EqualityWitness. The index's classification (context.parameters contains head || isEquality(head), a tag check) is exactly the non-zero condition of canDeriveCoercion (same `p == head` test; cast to EqualityWitness is a tag check). So canDeriveCoercions over ix.coercionSources returns the same Boolean as over all givens: the result is an OR, the non-sources contribute 0b00, and the memo keys are unchanged.
(P3) No assumed given in the environment has an equality head. A bare-parameter (universal) assumed premise would also be a source, but it cannot be written in source: a `<T>` annotation parses only as a lambda type; the attempt is in i04.

Under P1-P3, a skipped given has a nominal head k' != k = nominalHead(goal), with both non-nil. Its thread can never complete:
- A top-level shape mismatch (Struct/Enum/MachineType vs anything else, after unifiable dealiases both sides) yields either the unique pair (a,b), which fails at once, or a dealiased pair, which goes to canDeriveCoercions and gets false.
- Different abstractions under a TypeApplication (trait P vs trait Q) call canDeriveCoercions(Q,P,env). With no visible sources and no equality assumptions this is false, so the thread fails at its first match.
- Caveat (REPORT §5.3 is imprecise): if the skipped given's OWN context has an equality premise (`given <T,U where T == U> => Box<U> is Q`), formThread pushes that premise into the thread's environment. canDeriveCoercions(Q,P) is then true and the baseline thread survives the first step, possibly until maxImplicitDepth. It still cannot produce a result: discharging it needs a proof of Q ~ P between distinct nominal constructors, and with no equality givens and only refl/sym/trans builtins none exists. So `done`, its order and the minimal penalties are unchanged, though the baseline does more work. Checked with the oracle on i11 and t01/t15: identical, and baseline matches 363 vs 79 with index.

nominalHead is conservative for every head form, meaning anything it cannot classify returns nil and is treated as a wildcard or 'all':
- type variables, generic parameters, associated types, existentials, metatypes, tuples, arrows, remote types, bundles, higher-kinded applications (abstraction is a parameter or variable), generic aliases (TypeApplication of a TypeAlias), and aliases of traits used as abstractions;
- non-generic aliases resolve to the head of their aliasee, which matches unifiable's dealiasing.

Penalties: assumed givens get offsets 0..a-1 in reverse order, visible entries a+group, builtins a+groupCount. This is exactly the baseline. Entries are merged by position, so thread order, and with it `done` order and tie-breaking, is preserved.

Builtins (reflexivity/symmetry/transitivity, all with EqualityWitness heads) are skipped only when k != nil. They then fail with a top-level mismatch, so this is correct.

Evaluation order: building the index forces declaredType(of:) for all visible givens in group order. That is the same order baseline summon uses in the same scope. The only extra forcing is in coerced() -> canDeriveCoercions, where the baseline exits early. But a true answer is immediately followed by summon(T~U) in the same scope, which forces all givens in the same order, and a false answer has already iterated them all. So nothing observable intervenes; probes i01/i02/i09/i10 plus 16 permutations in perm/ confirmed this.

Fresh-variable numbering changes (fewer formThread instantiations), but variables never appear in the dump or diagnostics (they become #!). Checked in i03.

redundancy_notes: index and names target different costs, and their gains add up: names removes applies() calls, index cuts the per-subgoal scan of givens. index and absmodel share the indexedSummon entry point, and absmodel refutation runs first, so on refuted goals index's work is skipped. On breadth-style workloads index alone already brings matches close to the number of real candidates, so absmodel adds little there. loopcheck is orthogonal: it prunes repeated subgoals, while index prunes non-matching givens per subgoal. canDeriveCoercions benefits from index.coercionSources independently of summon. The proposed 'coesrc' and 'dtree' ideas overlap with index-2 and index-4. A discrimination tree over full heads would subsume the head-constructor bucketing, and a finer coercion-source test would remove most fallbacks in generic code with equality constraints.

- If both are TypeApplications, the first coercion pair is (k, k'), the two bare constructors. `match` calls canDeriveCoercions(k, k'), which uses the coercion-free `unifiable(_:_:)` (TypeStore.swift:965) against each source side.

The flag is true iff some coercion source has one of these:
(a) a bare context-parameter head (`<T> T`);
(b) an equality head where either side, after `open(context.parameters)` and alias unfolding, is a type variable or context parameter;
(c) an equality head where either side is an unapplied nominal constructor (Struct, Enum, Trait or MachineType), since only these sides can satisfy the coercion-free `unifiable(k, side)` for a bare constructor k.

Keep the second fallback for equality assumptions in `environment.givens` unchanged, and keep `canDeriveCoercions` using `ix.coercionSources`.

A more exact but more expensive alternative is to compute, per index, the set of head keys k for which `canDeriveCoercions(k, k')` can set both bits for some k' among `byHead.keys`, and fall back only when the goal's head is in that set.

soundness_argument:
Intended argument. Read each visible given `<X..> A1..An ==> H` as the Horn clause H :- A1..An. Every SummonResult that baseline resolution returns is a closed derivation. In it, every assumed given (pending sibling or ancestor premises, coercion equalities) has been discharged. These assumptions sit on a LIFO stack, and position i is discharged with only positions < i in the environment. So, by induction from the bottom of the stack, any derivation that is complete when no equality-headed or variable-headed given is visible proves only syntactically trivial equalities (equal modulo aliases and modulo the parts that abstract to ⊤). The final instance of every subgoal is therefore in the least Herbrand model of the visible user clauses, with equality premises counted as true. Ignoring environment givens in the model is sound for that reason. Pruning a subgoal that has no complete derivation removes only threads that can never reach `.done`. The BFS layer of the first result, maxImplicitDepth, minimalElements by penalty, and the summon memoisation therefore all stay the same. Equality goals are never refuted, and the model gives up (inconclusive) on ⊤, variable or equality heads. This covers every coercion source that canDeriveCoercion recognises. abstraction(of:) maps to ⊤ every type that the concrete unifier can match non-structurally or through a type variable: associated types, arrows, metatypes, remote types, bundles, existentials, opaque types, and higher-kinded applications.

The argument needs four implementation facts, and three of them are false in the code:
(i) Subsumption must never drop a needed fact. It does. `subsumes` treats ⊤ as a constant when it checks a nonlinear general variable, so R(v,v) 'subsumes' R(⊤,⊤) and R(S(⊤),S(⊤)), although ⊤ stands for terms that need not be equal. Confirmed wrong refutations: t03 (k=2, higher-kinded head) and t02/t23 (k≥3, ⊤ lifted by truncation).
(ii) Unification must terminate. It need not, because there is no occurs check. Bottom-up matching creates cyclic bindings that top-down search never creates, and `applying` then overflows the stack. The type checker crashes on valid programs (t01, t18).
(iii) The model for a scope must cover exactly the givens visible from it. The module-wide sharing at file scope breaks this when files of one module have different `import`s (code argument only; the oracle cannot build multi-module programs).
(iv) Saturation is sound modulo a variable-renaming collision when the work counter goes above about 4.19M per model (theoretical).

Everything else I checked holds. Truncation is monotone. Unification with ⊤ does not bind. Dropping premises that have a context is safe. Semi-naive rounds are complete, including incremental saturation started from the parent model. factLimit overflow falls back to inconclusive. Equality and variable goals are skipped. abstractClause and contextAndHead flatten nested contexts. Evaluating given types early in abstractModel runs only when declarationsOnStack is empty, and no divergence showed up on the 31 cycle-heavy `names` programs. Preconditions for soundness after the fixes: an occurs check (or ⊤ on a cycle) in unify, ⊤-aware subsumption, and a file-level cache key that includes the file's imports.
checked_ok: Equality goals are never refuted, and models with an equality head or a bare-variable head are inconclusive. This covers both coercion sources of canDeriveCoercion. t20-coercion-where (equalities in where clauses, nested scopes) is identical.
Ignoring environment (assumed) givens is sound by the LIFO discharge argument: sibling premises, ancestor premises and coercion equalities. t19-sibling-premise is identical.
Dropping premises that have a context and treating equality premises as satisfied is a valid over-approximation (code review).

abstraction(of:): associated types, arrows, metatypes, remote types, bundles, opaque and existential types, higher-kinded TypeApplications and generic-alias applications all map to ⊤. Plain TypeAlias is dealiased, matching unifiable(), which also dealiases. Rigid generic parameters become nodes, as in concrete unification. Tuples become cons/empty. t04, t05, t09, t12 are identical.
unify with ⊤ matches anything without binding, so the result over-approximates.

Semi-naive saturation (round 0 against old facts, delta/old split per premise, min(hi,count) cutoff) and incremental saturation from the parent model's facts are complete (code review). t06 (local scopes) and t07 (deep recursion) are identical.
factLimit overflow sets isInconclusive and stops; mayDerive then returns true.
Variable and equality queries are skipped (u.isVariable, key == .equality).
Nested (trait) givens and .recursive givens: contextAndHead flattens nested Universal and Implication types. t11-nested-givens and t13-cond-ext are identical.
Value givens and implicit value parameters (t10) are identical.
Pruning only removes threads that cannot reach .done, so the first BFS layer with results, maxImplicitDepth and the penalty-based selection are unchanged.

redundancy_notes: On the stdlib, `absmodel` alone cuts summon.matches from 41452 to 29955 (−28%), but on top of `index` only from 15051 to 14138 (−6%). Most of its stdlib benefit overlaps with the head-indexed candidate skipping. Its unique value is refuting whole doomed subgoals: the intro.md divergent and growing patterns. `loopcheck` covers only the identical-loop pattern (loopcheck prunes 0 on the stdlib). On generic-heavy user code (t26) it builds one model per function scope (151 builds) and refuted nothing, so it is pure overhead: about +0.7 s at k=2 and about +32 s at k=3. Cheap wins: default to k=2; skip or memoise per-scope rebuilds when local clauses add only premise-free rigid facts; index joins by the first argument. Memory grows as O(scopes × facts) because every scope model is cached as a separate copy.

info.title: Default depth k=3 makes saturation blow up (≈10 s on the stdlib, 30+ s on a generic-heavy user file) with no extra refutation
info.evidence:
TyperCounters.swift: `absDepth ... guard let p = getenv("HYLO_TC_ABSDEPTH") else { return 3 }`, while REPORT §5.4 recommends k=2. Rough counters on a shared, loaded machine (research/review/absmodel/counters-notes.txt):
- stdlib at k=3: absmodel.facts=14082, work=3,768,008, micros≈10.8 s, refuted=224.
- stdlib at k=2: facts=1399, work=14,783, ≈20 ms, refuted=225.
- t26-perf-many-scopes.hylo (150 generic functions, each with one local given): baseline type.user≈5.6 s; absmodel k=2 adds about 0.7 s and refutes nothing (built=151, summon.matches unchanged at 142500); absmodel k=3 gives type.user≈38 s (absmodel micros≈31.8 s, facts=413,159, work=639M).
Causes: (1) every scope that declares a given copies the parent's model and re-saturates. Sibling function scopes redo the same joins, and every per-scope model is cached (memory is O(scopes × facts)). (2) match() is an unindexed nested-loop join over whole buckets: a two-premise clause over R×R is quadratic in the bucket.
info.suggested_fix: Change the default absDepth to 2. Index buckets by the first argument's key, or use discrimination trees, for joins. Skip building a scope model when the new local clauses have premise-free heads that cannot enable new joins, or cap per-scope work and mark the model inconclusive. Consider not caching models for leaf function scopes.

info.title: Variable renaming offset in match() can collide with clause free variables once a model's work counter exceeds ~4.19M
info.evidence: AbstractResolution.swift match(): `let g = f.isGround ? f : f.offsettingVariables(by: (1 << 20) + (work << 8))`. Free type variables of a clause are numbered `(1 << 30) + i` in TypeStore.abstraction (`let v = (1 << 30) + variables.count`). When work ≥ (2^30 − 2^20)/256 ≈ 4,190,208, a renamed fact variable can equal a clause's free variable and wrongly bind it. That could lose facts or bind wrongly. `work` is carried over from the parent model (m = n), so it accumulates along the scope chain. On t26 at k=3 the average per-model work is already ≈4.2M (639M over 151 models). This only matters for givens whose declared type contains type variables (rare). Facts with more than 256 variables would also collide with the next offset. Not reproduced.
info.suggested_fix: Rename fact variables with a dedicated fresh counter in a disjoint range (e.g. negative integers), or reserve the clause range by offsetting the clause variables instead.

verified.title: Subsumption in insert() treats ⊤ as a constant for nonlinear variables and drops facts that are needed, so derivable goals are refuted
verified.evidence:
AbstractResolution.swift subsumes(): `case (.variable(let v), _): if let u = s[v] { return u == t }`. With general R(v,v) and specific R(⊤,⊤) (or R(S(⊤),S(⊤))), v binds to ⊤ and the second occurrence compares ⊤ == ⊤, which is true. The specific fact is dropped, although ⊤ denotes uncorrelated terms. Facts with ⊤ above the truncation depth come from higher-kinded heads (F<A> → ⊤, at any k) or from truncation lifted through a variable (premise W<T> matched against Q(W(S(⊤))) binds T := S(⊤); this needs k ≥ 3, and the code default is 3). - research/review/absmodel/oracle_subsume_k2.txt, t03-subsume-hk-k2.hylo: MISMATCH. Baseline resolves `Z is W<Y>` (node 0:64 -> need). absmodel adds `error: no coercion from 'W<Z, Y> ==> [Void]() let -> Void' to '[Void]() let -> Void'`.
- oracle_subsume_k3.txt, t02-subsume-top-k3.hylo: the same kind of mismatch at k=3.
- oracle_t23_k3.txt, t23-subsume-trunc-k3.hylo has no higher-kinded types. Givens: `W<S<Box<A>>> is Q`, `W<S<Crate<B>>> is Q`, `<T> T is R<T>`, `<T,U where W<T> is Q, W<U> is Q> T is R<U>`. For example: `if let u = s[v] { return u == t && !t.containsTop && !u.containsTop }`. Alternatively, skip subsumption entirely for specific facts that contain ⊤ below a nonlinear variable. A valid program is rejected, so this breaks the soundness definition.

The code confirms the mechanism. In AbstractResolution.swift, subsumes() (line 312) does `case (.variable(let v), _): if let u = s[v] { return u == t }`. This compares a ⊤-containing binding with plain syntactic equality, but each ⊤ stands for an independent, unknown term. So R(v,v) (from `<T> T is R<T>`) is taken to subsume R(S(⊤),S(⊤)), and insert() (line 226) drops the second fact.

Trace for t23 at k=3:
1. Truncation at depth 3 turns W<S<Box<A>>> into Q(W(S(⊤))).
2. The clause `<T,U where W<T> is Q, W<U> is Q> T is R<U>` binds T and U to S(⊤) and yields R(S(⊤),S(⊤)).
3. That fact is dropped as subsumed by R(v,v).
4. mayDerive (lines 115-124) does not truncate the query. R(S(Box(A)),S(Crate(B))) then fails to unify with R(v,v): v binds to S(Box(A)), and S(Crate(B)) does not match it.
5. The query is wrongly refuted, and the false "no coercion" error is reported.

For t03, the ⊤ comes from the higher-kinded head F<A>, which abstraction() maps to .top. That is why t03 triggers already at k=2.

unify() itself is fine: unify(var, ⊤) does not bind, which over-approximates. The defect is only in the subsumption check.

Two parts of the finding are wrong, but neither changes the verdict:
- t15-subsume-hk-order.hylo is NOT affected. It is identical at both k=2 and k=3, in the old oracle_subsume_k2.txt and in my re-run.
- t23 is identical to the baseline at k=2; it diverges only at k=3.

verdict.fix:
In AbstractResolution.swift, add to the Term extension:

`fileprivate var containsTop: Bool { switch self { case .top: true; case .variable: false; case .node(_, let xs): xs.contains(where: \.containsTop) } }`

Then in subsumes() change the variable case to:

`case (.variable(let v), _): if let u = s[v] { return u == t && !t.containsTop }; s[v] = t; return true`

A repeated variable of the general fact must never be matched against a ⊤-containing subterm, because separate ⊤ occurrences are uncorrelated. A variable that occurs once may still bind ⊤. The result stays conservative: refusing to subsume only keeps more facts.

Simpler alternative: skip subsumption whenever the specific fact contains ⊤ and the general fact is nonlinear (has a repeated variable).

Also:
- Add t02, t03 and t23 as positive regression tests, and run them under absmodel at k=2 and k=3.
- Correct REPORT.md §5.4 ("Over-approximations, all sound").
- Remove t15 from the list of affected programs.

verified.title: No occurs check in the abstract unifier: bottom-up saturation builds cyclic bindings and the type checker crashes (SIGSEGV, stack overflow) on valid programs
verified.evidence:
AbstractResolution.unify has no occurs check ('mirroring the concrete unifier'). In bottom-up evaluation, the premise P(T, S(T)) of `given <T where T is P<S<T>>> => T is R` is matched against the fact P(U,U) of `given <U> => U is P<U>`. soundness_argument:
The REPORT argues the change is sound because (a) errors only grow along a branch, so a candidate with errors at quiescence can never reach an error-free solution, and (b) committing a sole survivor in place does what the baseline's only viable fork would do. Both arguments quietly assume the solver is confluent, meaning the order in which goals are processed does not change the result. The Hylo solver is not confluent:
(i) The first binding of a type variable wins. Unifying %t with X and then with A<Void> leaves %t = X; the other order leaves %t = A<Void>.
(ii) Coercions into a join variable bind it to whichever argument is processed first. With `where T == U`, that decides which argument receives a coercion witness, and whether a later syntactic equality (from widening with `as`) still holds.
(iii) Synthetic witness nodes are numbered in the order elaborations are made.
(iv) Ranking is nested. solve(overload:) ranks only the set it branches on, using isPreferred over the viable solutions, so which set sits at the outer level changes the winner, and whether the result is a unique choice or an ambiguity.
The flag changes the order in three ways:
- It parks every OverloadConstraint until the fresh stack is empty. The baseline forks the moment the constraint is popped.
- It defers refreshCoercionAndWideningConstraints until all parked sets are resolved.
- It branches on the parked set with the fewest survivors first, and commits the first set that has a sole survivor, regardless of how deep it is.
In addition, scoring is inconsistent: probes and cancellation use current.errors, while solve(overload:) ranks by diagnostics.count. Nested "ambiguous use" diagnostics are not counted in current.errors. So the baseline can keep, and even prefer, a candidate that has errors when the error-free candidate carries a nested ambiguity, and pruning that candidate changes the diagnostics.

Precondition for an exact, dump-identical version (none of this has been compiled or tested; building is forbidden here):
(1) Do not park. Run forward checking at the moment the baseline would fork, when the OverloadConstraint is popped.
(2) Each probe forks from that state and runs the same goal sequence as the baseline fork until the next OverloadConstraint is popped or the fresh stack is empty. Stop there: no parking and no coercion defaulting inside a probe. Probe errors are then a prefix of the errors of every baseline sub-branch, so pruning drops only candidates whose current.errors is at least 1 in every baseline continuation.
(3) Keep the baseline's branching order. Drop most-constrained-first.
(4) Commit by running solve(overload: g, among: survivors), with the survivors in their original order, as a fork. If the solution it returns has 0 diagnostics, return it. Otherwise re-run the full baseline solve(overload: g) over all candidates. If the winning solution has no diagnostics, the baseline's viable list provably reduces to the same entries: pruned candidates are either cancelled, since current is greater than best = 0, or erased when the 0-diagnostic solution resets the list. The decisions made inside each fork also do not depend on the inherited `best`.
(5) Restore the baseline coercion defaulting: call refreshCoercionAndWideningConstraints whenever the fresh stack becomes empty outside probe mode.
Steps (1) and (2) alone fix overload-priority.hylo, s18 and t19. Step (3) fixes s15, t02, t03 and t13. Step (4) fixes t01, s01, t15 and t16. Whether ovl/ovr still get their speedup depends on whether each call's argument coercion comes before the next OverloadConstraint on the fresh stack. That needs to be measured. If it does not, keep parking inside probes, but prune only on errors recorded before the first nested parking.
checked_ok: Commit in place with a truly sole survivor sets the same outcomes[g] (delegate([equality])) and bindings[k.name] as the baseline fork. Not updating the parent's `best` has no effect, because the baseline returns (terminated) right after solve(overload:).
Probe cancellation (a nil score) only happens when current > best, which implies at least 1 error, so excluding cancelled candidates from the scores never drops a clean candidate.
Probes never run resolveParked or coercion defaulting (they return when the fresh stack is empty), so they do not branch.
The fallback when no probe has 0 errors keeps all k.candidates.
Penalties are never incremented anywhere (always 0), so the solver's use of current.penalties cannot diverge.

Identical on: t04 (closures plus higher-order generic, erroneous in both), t05 (operators with literals), t11 (tuples and member chains), t12 (conditional conformance with a where-constrained extension), t14 (lambdas against an overloaded higher-order callee), t17 (valid literal overloads), t18 (s18 with k overloaded), s16 (equal survivor counts keep the baseline order), s27, and prior s05-s09, s19-s25.
The combined config of all six flags gives the same mismatches as solver alone on t09-t19, so no new interaction appeared.
redundancy_notes: solver does not overlap with names, unify, index, absmodel or loopcheck: those speed up name lookup, unification and implicit resolution, while solver only changes how overload sets are searched. Its benefit is limited to expressions with several overload sets, such as the ovl and ovr workloads (forks 448 -> 0 and 1092 -> 0). On the stdlib it is pure overhead: no pruning, no commits, +12% goal steps and 48 times more refresh scans. A sound variant should be gated so that small sets and single-set systems skip probing. Component decomposition (the next step proposed in the REPORT) would add the same nesting-order hazard as most-constrained-first unless ranking and ambiguity are defined per component.

soundness_argument:
The claim in REPORT.md §5.5: in a smallest derivation, no subgoal is identical to one of its ancestors, because the ancestor's derivation could be replaced by the subgoal's. That would give a smaller term that finishes in an earlier BFS layer, so pruning such subgoals never removes the result the baseline picks (first non-empty layer, then minimal penalties).

This replacement argument (Bol–Apt–Klop's equality check) only holds when the subgoal's derivation uses nothing that is unavailable at the ancestor. Hylo resolution breaks that assumption. In threadContinuation (Typer.swift ~3797-3810) the last pending premise is summoned in an environment that still contains the not-yet-discharged sibling premises as assumed givens. summon() puts `environment.givens` first as candidates (line ~3663; indexedSummon ~4071). So the derivation of an inner subgoal identical to its ancestor `G` can use a pending sibling premise `p` of an ancestor's given as a hypothesis. That hypothesis is discharged later. The resulting term is a let-shared DAG, e.g. g1(D_P, g3(g4(p), g5(p))) with p := D_P. Its match count is 1+1+2+2+|D_P|. The direct tree g3(g4(D_P), g5(D_P)) costs 1+2(1+|D_P|).

So the derivation through the "loop" can be strictly shorter, or the same length with lower penalties, than any loop-free derivation. Pruning it changes:
(a) which witness wins, by layer or by penalty;
(b) whether the result is ambiguous;
(c) whether a result exists within maxImplicitDepth = 10, giving a new "no given instance" error.

All three are confirmed by the oracle (see findings).

When the technique is sound: when no hypothesis is introduced between the ancestor and the subgoal, i.e. environment.givens at the subgoal is the same stack as at the ancestor (no pending sibling premises and no coercion-assumed equalities). In that case the pure-SLD lifting argument applies. Already-solved siblings that bind variables do not break this: by lifting, a derivation of Gσ yields a no-longer derivation of G, so the baseline finishes in an earlier layer anyway. Comparing on reified types when variables are bound later is conservative: pruning only happens on identity at check time, so later bindings can only miss prunes, never add wrong ones.

Ancestry bookkeeping per thread is correct. Environment is a value type copied per fork. Ancestry is keyed by the unique assumed-given id: nextGivenIdentifier is never decremented, and removeValue happens on discharge. assuming(given:) and assuming(givens:) copy the dictionary. Coercion-assumed equality givens get no ancestry entry, which is conservative. The top-level goal is included through formThread(ancestors: []).appending(queried).

Here g1's pending premise `SP is T` (p) is reused inside the inner derivation: g1(D_P, g3(g4(p), g5(p))). The loop term then costs the same as the direct term g3(g4(D_P), g5(D_P)): 9 matches each, as the finding claims. So loop terms are genuine minimum-cost candidates in the baseline's metric. Two copies of g1 give two such candidates, and the baseline reports an ambiguity. Loopcheck removes both, and only the direct term is left. verdict.fix:
Prune at Typer.swift:3642 only when the ancestor's derivation cannot gain anything from a pending sibling premise. Concretely:

1. When an implication is unfolded (Typer.swift:3721), record in the ancestry entry the identifiers of all assumed givens introduced by that same formThread unfolding, that is, the sibling premises of the looping given.
2. In the loopcheck test, skip pruning if any assumed given in environment.givens was introduced at or below the matching ancestor and is not the cycle premise itself. Equivalently, prune only when the looping given's context has exactly one premise, or none of its other premises is still pending or assumed.

This keeps the intro.md pattern `forall T. P T ==> P T` (single premise) and the Loop/Dead workloads pruned. It turns pruning off for multi-premise loops like lc06/lc07 and the LC-1 shared-lemma cases, where a pending sibling premise lets the loop term tie with or beat the direct term.

A simpler sound fallback is to prune only when the environment has no assumed givens except the cycle premise itself.

soundness_argument:
This review checks REPORT.md's claims. It does not review a single technique. Each technique's soundness as the report states it, with the correct preconditions:

(1) absmodel. Summon only returns real derivations. Pending premises used as hypotheses are themselves discharged later. Built-in equalities and coercions are covered by the 'equality goal => may derive', 'equality premise => satisfied' and 'equality- or variable-headed user given => inconclusive' rules. Depth-k truncation is a homomorphism into a finite domain (Sato–Tamaki). So a goal that unifies with no abstract fact has no derivation, whatever the size order or depth cap.
- Pruning a thread that can never complete does not change the first BFS layer that completes, nor the penalties chosen there.
- Preconditions: the abstract clause set must be a superset of every candidate summon can use, including nested trait givens, header conformances and local givens. Aliases must be resolved. Higher-kinded and associated types must become ⊤.
- I found no counterexample: 28 new or rerun programs are dump-identical.
- What it cannot refute: divergence whose facts survive truncation (t/div-nested-grow.hylo, t/div-loop-under-ctor.hylo), and every depth-cap failure.

(2) loopcheck. The report argues that 'an ancestor's subderivation can be replaced by the identical descendant's, giving a smaller term'. That only holds if cost is tree size. In this engine cost is the number of BFS match steps, and pending sibling premises act as shared hypotheses. A derivation that repeats a goal can therefore take fewer steps than every loop-free one. The claim is false: the oracle shows mismatches on lc04, lc05 and lc06.

(3) names is not semantics-preserving. applies() has memoisation side effects under cycle cuts (confirmed on n04).

(4) solver's claim that 'the original order of decisions is preserved' is false: overload-priority.hylo node 0:75 gets type A<Void> instead of X.

(5) index: the fallback conditions in the code match the stated preconditions: no coercion sources, no non-assumed or equality-headed assumed givens, nothing on the stack.

(6) The depth cap bounds BFS steps. That count is roughly proof-tree size, plus one root coercion step, minus pending-premise sharing. It does not bound height.
- So the report's statement 'The cap measures thread steps, not term size' is misleading.
- The proposed minimum-height bound (Knuth with 1+max) is sound but almost never fires.
- Removing the cap through tabling is not safe, because neither absmodel nor loopcheck stops div-nested-grow.

verdict.reasoning:
I re-ran the cases on the frozen baseline binary (`tc-bench --count`, no flags). The output is saved in /home/user/hylo-new/research/review/claims/verify-C1/rerun.txt.
- chain9: summon.depthExhausted=1 and the 'no coercion from P<S^9<Z>> ...' error.
- wide-given-8: accepted at summon.layers=10.
- wide-given-9 (one given with 9 premises, proof height 2): rejected with depthExhausted=1.

- c07-shared-premise-height: accepted at layers=8.
I also wrote a new test, verify-C1/wide9-sep.hylo, which puts the 9 premises directly on the function's where-clause. It is accepted because each requirement is summoned on its own and uses at most 10 layers. So the cap is per summon call. It bounds the steps of one derivation, not the program.

Code check, Typer.swift:3743-3810 and 3846-3865:
- Each `match` call is one BFS layer.
- A successful match goes to `threadContinuation`. That function discharges only the last pending assumption (`thread.environment.givens.last`) and pushes the next `summon` as a new thread for the following layer. So the premises of a given are solved one after another along a single thread.
- A thread that finishes at layer d therefore used d steps. That is about one per node of the proof tree, plus the root match. Premises that equal a pending assumption cost one step (c07). A match that needs a coercion costs one extra layer (`.next([thread.copy(...)])`), so the step count can also be larger than the tree size.

So the cap bounds steps, which is roughly the size of the proof, not its height. REPORT §6.1 says "The cap measures thread steps, not term size". Read as "steps differ from size", that is misleading, because the steps are about the term size. lit-resolution.md §0 and §1.4 describe this correctly.

The min-height recommendation (§5.4 and §7.3) is sound, since steps ≥ height, but weak. It cannot predict wide-given-9, c05 or the wide-tuple failures, whose heights are 2-3.

One overstatement in the finding: chain9 may be predictable. It depends on the convention. If the bound counts the extra root step (layers for chain8 = 10 = nodes + 1), chain9 needs 11 > 10 and would be flagged. "Predicts none of the cases" is therefore true only for a plain node-height bound.

Side observation: a given with n identical premises makes the baseline blow up exponentially.
- verify-C1/shared6.hylo: 89,856 matches.
- verify-C1/shared10.hylo and shared9.hylo (12 premises): crash at the 2.5 GB cap with 'failed to allocate'.
Each identical premise can be discharged both by the pending assumption and by the real given, so the threads probably fork 2^n times. This looks like a real baseline performance bug, worth recording separately.

I rate the finding minor rather than major. It concerns the accuracy of the report and a weak recommendation, not the type checker's behavior.
verdict.fix:
Changes to REPORT.md:
1. Reword §6.1: "The cap bounds the number of match steps along one resolution thread within a single summon. That is roughly the proof-tree size plus one root step. It is lower when a premise is discharged by a pending assumption and higher by one per coercion match. So a height-2 proof with 9 or more premises (wide-given-9) is also rejected."
2. In §5.4 and §7.3, say that the minimum-height bound is sound but only catches deep chains, and only if it counts the extra root step (the cap is passed when h_nodes + 1 > maxImplicitDepth).
3. To predict wide failures, use a sound lower bound on steps instead. Option: Knuth's algorithm with a 1+min-cost sum over premises, where the minimum is taken over the alternative givens. Repeated premises that can be shared make this an overestimate, so either discount premises that are syntactically identical to a pending one, or count only distinct premises. Applied as an admissible prune in takeSummonResults (steps so far + remaining lower bound > cap), it is sound under the current semantics.
4. Better, redefine the cap as a height or depth limit, or replace it with tabled resolution as §7.4 already proposes. That would be a semantic change and must be flagged as one.
5. Separately, record the baseline blow-up for n identical premises (verify-C1/shared6.hylo, shared10.hylo). Fix it by not forking a second thread when a premise is discharged by an identical pending assumption, or by deduplicating identical premises in a given's where-clause.

I re-ran the repro on the frozen baseline binary 4587ce9e1a23 with no flags set. For /home/user/hylo-new/research/review/claims/verify-C2/c10-tuple-copy-real.hylo, the baseline accepts `dup` on the 4-tuple and rejects it on the 5-tuple with "error: no coercion from '<T> Copyable<T> ==> [Void](let T) let -> T' to '[Void](let {Bool, Bool, Bool, Bool, Bool}) ...'". So the search was cut off, not exhausted. The stdlib conformance `given <T is Copyable, U is Copyable> => {T, ...U} is Copyable` (StandardLibrary/Sources/Core/Copyable.hylo:15) proves any tuple of Copyable elements. It works for 3-tuples (15 layers) and 4-tuples (17 layers).

The problem is wider than the reported case. My new repros in /home/user/hylo-new/research/review/claims/verify-C2/:
- direct5.hylo: plain `c.copy()` on a 5-tuple of Bool fails with "type '{Bool, Bool, Bool, Bool, Bool}' has no member 'copy'" (depthExhausted=2).
- pair-nested.hylo: `dup(((true,false),(true,false),true))` fails the same way. A 3-tuple whose elements are pairs already exceeds the cap.

The `layers` counter is shared by the whole breadth-first resolution, and premises are resolved one after another through continuations. So the cap limits the total size of the proof (about two layers per tuple element), not the height of the proof tree.

The oracle (verify-C2/oracle.txt) prints 3/3 identical for each of names, unify, index, absmodel, solver and loopcheck, and for all six together. So this is a limitation of the baseline that no flag fixes or changes, as the finding says. The finding is right that this is not a synthetic chain: it blocks ordinary tuple copies. It is a baseline correctness bug, not a soundness issue with any optimization. I did not test a binary with a higher cap: the rules forbid building one, and claims/depth11-results.txt holds no 5-tuple result. The cap explanation rests on the depthExhausted counter and the code reading above.
verdict.fix:
Make the depth bound measure proof height, not the global count of breadth-first layers. Give each ResolutionThread its own height, counting how many givens' premises the thread has descended into, so that resolving sibling premises one after another through the continuation does not add to it. Then cap that height in place of the global `depth` in takeSummonResults (Typer.swift:3848). Also keep a separate, much larger budget on total steps or matches so that divergent searches still stop.

A stronger option is to detect real non-termination with a cycle check: a goal that recurs with a non-decreasing size along one branch (the loopcheck idea). Keep a large backstop cap as well.

Do not just raise maxImplicitDepth. The search is breadth-first and its cost is exponential in depth (12360 matches already at the 5-tuple), and that would still fail on 6- or 7-tuples.

This changes accepted programs, so it is a language fix, not a sound optimization. Land it on main separately from the optimization stack, re-freeze the oracle baseline after it, and add regression tests: dup and .copy() on 5- and 8-tuples, and on nested tuples. Finding 6.1 in REPORT.md should be elevated with this example.

verified.title: loopcheck soundness argument (§5.5, attributed to Bol–Apt–Klop) is false for this engine
verified.evidence:
I reran the oracle (/home/user/hylo-new/research/review/claims/oracle-loopcheck-lc04-06.txt): [loopcheck] 0/3 identical.
- lc04-cap-witness: the baseline witness c98 disappears and a new error appears, 'no given instance of T<SA>'.
- lc05-shared-lemma-penalty: a different witness term is selected.
- lc06-ambiguity-call: a baseline error disappears.

Cause: the candidates include pending premises (Typer.swift `gs.append(contentsOf: environment.givens.reversed()...)` in summon). A derivation that repeats a goal can reuse a pending premise and take fewer steps than any loop-free one. In lc04 that is 10 steps against 11, past the cap. So the claim 'grafting the inner subtree gives a smaller term that completes in an earlier layer' fails.

lit-resolution.md §3.10 even says 'check that a pending assumption doesn't make the shortcut cheaper (it can only make it cheaper)', which is the wrong way round. The same section admits that the argument is the author's own reasoning (§6 'Things I could not verify'). The BAK paper was not downloaded, and BAK's soundness results concern existence of solutions for restricted program classes, not preservation of the selected minimal answer.
verified.suggested_fix: Mark loopcheck unsound in §5.5 and §7.3. Either restrict pruning to cases with no pending premises in the environment and no depth-cap interaction, or drop it in favour of absmodel or tabling. Correct the attribution: BAK motivates loop checks but does not prove this minimality-preservation property.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute this finding. I re-ran the oracle myself; the output is in /home/user/hylo-new/research/review/claims/verify-C3/oracle-rerun.txt. The configs `loopcheck;absmodel;index` were run on research/review/loopcheck/lc04-cap-witness.hylo, lc05-shared-lemma-penalty.hylo and lc06-ambiguity-call.hylo.
- **loopcheck: 0/3 identical.** absmodel and index were 3/3 identical, so the divergence comes from loopcheck alone.
- **lc04:** the baseline's `witness.c98` uses the loop instance (line 23, `SP is T, SA is T => SA is T`). With loopcheck that witness is gone and a new error appears: "no given instance of 'T<SA>'".
- **lc05:** a different witness is chosen. The baseline picks the loop term headed by line 24. Loopcheck picks the direct term headed by line 18.
- **lc06:** the baseline reports a "no coercion" error on `need()` because it finds two equally good loop terms. With loopcheck that error is gone and the call resolves.

None of these is a case where the baseline is broken. Every baseline result is a valid, deterministic elaboration. So under the given definition of sound, loopcheck is unsound.

**Mechanism, checked in the code (Sources/FrontEnd/Typer/Typer.swift):**
- **Pending premises are candidates.** `summon(...where:)` at l.3663 puts the pending premises (`environment.givens`) first among the candidates, with the smallest penalty offset. Using one costs a single match.
- **Cost counts BFS layers, not term size.** `takeSummonResults` (l.3845-3864) stops at the first BFS layer that has any result, with `maxImplicitDepth = 10`, and then keeps the minimal penalties. So the cost of a derivation is its number of matches, where a reused pending premise counts once. It is not the size of the elaborated term.
- **The dump shows the gap.** The baseline lc04/lc05 witnesses are textually much larger than the direct ones. The derivation of `SP` is inlined twice, once for each use of the premise `p`. Yet the search found them in fewer or equal layers.

**Why the §5.5 argument fails:** "Replace the ancestor's derivation by the subgoal's, giving a smaller term that completes in an earlier BFS layer" does not hold. The inner subtree may use premises introduced by steps on the path between the outer goal and the repeated inner goal. Grafting it at the outer position loses those premises, so the grafted derivation must re-derive them. It can then cost more layers (lc04: 11 against 10, past the cap, so the result is lost entirely), equal layers with higher penalties (lc05), or remove a tie that the baseline reports as an ambiguity (lc06).

**On the literature claim:** lit-resolution.md §3.10 says a pending assumption "can only make it cheaper, so the argument still holds". That is backwards: it makes the loop derivation cheaper, which is exactly what breaks the argument. §6 ("Things I could not verify") admits that the §3.10 soundness argument is the author's own reasoning, and §3.10 marks the BAK paper "Not downloaded". BAK's notion of soundness is that no solution is lost in unbounded SLD-style search. That covers neither preserving the selected minimal answer under a (layers, penalties) order nor a depth cap. Even BAK-style existence fails here only because of the cap (lc04). Minimality and ambiguity fail without the cap (lc05, lc06).

**Remaining text in REPORT.md:** the claim "Diagnostics are identical on all tests" in §5.5 is true only for the test corpus. §7.3 recommends adopting loopcheck and should be withdrawn or qualified.

**Nuance:** lc04 does interact with the depth cap. That is not a broken baseline, though: the baseline succeeds within the cap and loopcheck fails. lc05 and lc06 do not depend on the cap.
verdict.fix:
1. **Correct the documentation.** Mark loopcheck unsound in REPORT.md §5.5 and withdraw it from §7.3. Fix lit-resolution.md §3.10: a pending premise makes the loop derivation cheaper, which breaks the grafting argument rather than supporting it. Restate the BAK attribution as motivation only: BAK concerns not losing solutions in unbounded search, not keeping the selected (layers, penalties)-minimal answer or ambiguity reporting under a depth cap. Cite lc04/lc05/lc06 as counterexamples.

2. **Restrict the pruning so the grafting argument holds again.**
   - **Rule:** prune a subgoal G equal to an ancestor A only if no pending premise in the current environment was introduced by a step on the path from A down to G. In code: record `environment.nextGivenIdentifier` when A's implication is unfolded in `formThread`. In `summon(...where:)`, skip the prune if any assumed given with an identifier at or above that mark is still pending in `environment.givens`.
   - **Why it works:** under this rule the inner subtree uses only premises that are also available at A's position. Grafting then strictly removes matches and penalty terms, so the grafted derivation finishes in a strictly earlier layer. That keeps both the cap behaviour and the minimal result, and the loop term was never a minimal tie, so ambiguity is unaffected.
   - **Check before landing:** this restriction removes the benefit whenever the looping instance has more than one premise. Re-measure its benefit on the Loop/Dead workloads, and gate it with the oracle on lc01–lc15 plus the full corpus before re-adding it.

3. **Prefer replacing it.** Rely on absmodel (refutation, already 3/3 identical on these programs) for fail-fast. For the long term, use tabled resolution with an explicit sharing-aware cost (as REPORT §7.4 proposes), which handles cycles without changing which answer is selected.
